title: From 'The Next Step' to 'A Sad Day': Copia's Retreat from Uganda
dek: In 2023 Copia, which sold goods to rural Kenyans through village shop agents, left Uganda to make its home business pay; thirteen months later it entered administration.

story.event: Leaving Uganda to concentrate on profit in Kenya, then entering administration when new capital could not be raised
story.summary: In April 2023 Copia Global, the Kenyan company founded in 2013 by Tracey Turner and Jonathan Lewis to sell everyday goods to rural households through shopkeeper agents, closed its two-year-old Uganda operation to concentrate on making its Kenyan business profitable. After further job cuts and a $20 million extension, it entered administration in May 2024 when it could not raise capital on terms its stakeholders accepted; 1,060 jobs ended in June 2024 and the High Court ordered Copia Kenya into liquidation in September 2026.
paragraphs: In April 2023 Copia Global began telling its agents and customers in Uganda that it was leaving. The company, started in Kenya in 2013 by Tracey Turner and Jonathan Lewis, sold everyday goods to rural and small-town households through local shopkeepers who acted as agents: a customer chose from a Copia catalogue, the agent placed the order, and the goods arrived at the shop days later. When Copia opened in Uganda in 2021, Turner had called it "the next step" towards reaching Africa's emerging middle class. Its $50 million round of January 2022 had been raised to expand across the continent.

By early 2023 the company expected the economic downturn and tight capital markets to last. It chose to give up Uganda and, in its own words, "double down" on making its founding Kenyan business profitable. More than 350 people in Uganda lost their jobs, with severance, and agents were paid the commissions they were owed. "This is the right move for Copia given the market environment," said the chief executive, Tim Steel. In July about 350 of roughly 1,800 staff in Kenya were cut. Turner later called the Uganda exit "a sad day", saying investors would not fund Copia into new markets to profitability.

For a while the narrower plan held. In December 2023 investors added a $20 million extension, citing the turn towards profit in Kenya. In February 2024 Turner told Business Daily that Copia had 36,000 delivery points and a record of doubling its growth each year. On 16 May a memo warned staff of a possible shutdown or about 1,060 job cuts. On 24 May Makenzi Muthusi and Julius Ngonga of KPMG were appointed administrators; the parent company said it had been unable to attract capital "on terms that were amenable to all existing stakeholders". The 1,060 jobs ended on 7 June, after May salaries had been paid late.

The administrators then spent two years trying to rescue the business or sell its assets. On 17 September 2026 the High Court in Nairobi ordered Copia Kenya into liquidation, finding no realistic prospect of rescue, and rejected a supplier's allegations against the administrators as unsupported. They had told the court that, at best, only preferential creditors, employees among them, might receive anything.

quote.text: Steadfast a lamp burns sheltered from the wind; Such is the likeness of the Yogi's mind Shut from sense-storms and burning bright to Heaven.
quote.locator: Chapter VI, "Atmasanyamayog, or The Book of Religion by Self-Restraint" (verse 19 in the usual numbering)
quote.source_title: The Song Celestial; Or, Bhagavad-Gîtâ, tr. Sir Edwin Arnold, Project Gutenberg eBook #2388
quote.connection: The Gita's lamp holds steady because it is shut away from the wind. Copia pulled back to Kenya looking for that kind of shelter, but a company that needs new capital cannot close the window on the market, and the story leaves that tension standing.

reflection: Copia's retreat from Uganda was done with some care: people were told, severance was paid, agents got their commissions. It was a sensible narrowing, and it was still not enough. Both things are true, and neither cancels the other.

You will narrow things too: a feature dropped, a client turned down, an evening kept free. What the Gita's lamp suggests is that steadiness comes from what you can shelter, which is mostly your own attention. The winds that decide funding rounds or budgets are not yours to shut out. It helps to know which is which before a hard week, not in the middle of one.

sources.supports: At least 1,060 employees laid off two weeks after administration; termination letters to be signed on 7 June; May salaries paid late; orders stopped in six Kenyan locations.

sources.supports: Justice Rhoda Rutto's order of 17 September 2026 putting Copia Kenya into liquidation; no realistic prospect of rescue; administrators' statement that at best only preferential creditors, including employees, may receive a distribution; the 1,060 jobs ending on 7 June 2024; Uganda put on hold in April 2023; total funding counts of $107 million (2024) and $123 million.

cross_checks.claim: Copia was founded in Kenya in 2013 by Tracey Turner and Jonathan Lewis.
Copia opened in Uganda in 2021 and closed the operation in April 2023 to concentrate on profitability in Kenya, affecting more than 300 (company: more than 350) employees.
About 350 of roughly 1,800 Kenyan staff were cut in July 2023.
Copia entered administration on 24 May 2024 with KPMG's Makenzi Muthusi and Julius Ngonga as administrators, after failing to raise capital, and 1,060 jobs ended in early June 2024.
On 17 September 2026 the High Court ordered Copia Kenya into liquidation and rejected a creditor's allegations against the administrators.

research_notes: This edition is Copia's own episode, distinct from the Sendy and Twiga Foods editions: a rural, agent-based consumer retailer that retreated from Uganda to make its home market pay. Uganda launch: TechCabal, Techweez and TechMoran say 2021; Citizen Digital says 2018 and a Techweez 2026 timeline says 2022; the story uses 2021. Uganda job losses: the company (via TechCabal) said more than 350; Techweez and TechMoran said over 300; a former employee quoted by TechCabal in 2024 said 700 for the whole scaling-back. The story uses the company's 'more than 350'. July 2023: Citizen Digital reports about 350 of 1,800 workers; the company said less than 25% of the permanent workforce; TechMoran says over 800 across Kenya and Uganda in total. Final layoffs: TechCabal, Launch Base Africa and tech-ish give 1,060; Techweez (June 2024) said 'all remaining 1,500'; the story uses 1,060. Total funding varies from $103 million over seven rounds (Crunchbase via TechCabal, 2023) to 'over $100 million' over eight (Launch Base Africa, 2024), $107 million (tech-ish's 2024 count) and $123 million (TechCabal, Techweez, tech-ish 2026); the story gives only the $50 million and $20 million rounds. Causes are given only as the company and Turner put them (economic downturn, constrained capital markets, inability to raise on agreeable terms); analysts' views on unit economics are left out, and so is Techweez's 2025 speculation about the founders' later ventures. Founders' roles: Turner was co-founder and chair, Tim Steel the chief executive who announced the Uganda decision; Jonathan Lewis is not quoted in any source found. On creditors, tech-ish notes that the administrators' report put realisable assets (KES 206.6 million) above claims (KES 169.5 million) while the administrators told the court liabilities exceed assets; the story reports only the administrators' statement to the court. TechCabal pages were read by a plain request with the verifier's user agent because the fetch tool was refused; the Business Daily interview was read from the identical Nation Media copy at mwanaspoti.co.tz. The Gita line is about the disciplined mind, applied here by analogy.
